title: One Missed Separation, One Extra Chromosome

scenes.tts: In 1959, a laboratory in Paris counted the chromosomes in cells from nine children with Down syndrome. It found forty-seven, not the usual forty-six. One chromosome too many. How does a cell end up with an extra one? The answer begins in meiosis, when a pair of chromosomes fails to part.
scenes.caption: In 1959, a laboratory in Paris counted the chromosomes in cells from nine children with Down syndrome. It found 47, not the usual 46. One chromosome too many. How does a cell end up with an extra one? The answer begins in meiosis, when a pair of chromosomes fails to part.
scenes.visual: A cell holds 46 small chromosomes under a counter reading 46; a 47th appears in red and the counter changes, with a question mark.
scenes.narration: In 1959, a laboratory in Paris counted the chromosomes in cells from nine children with Down syndrome. It found 47, not the usual 46. One chromosome too many. How does a cell end up with an extra one? The answer begins in meiosis, when a pair of chromosomes fails to part.

scenes.tts: A cell makes sperm or eggs in two divisions. At meiosis one, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis two, the two sister chromatids of each chromosome separate. Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. Where it happens changes the result.
scenes.caption: A cell makes sperm or eggs in two divisions. At meiosis I, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis II, the two sister chromatids of each chromosome separate. Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. Where it happens changes the result.
scenes.visual: One cell with a blue and a yellow homologue splits at meiosis I into two cells, one homologue each, then at meiosis II into four, one chromatid each.
scenes.narration: A cell makes sperm or eggs in two divisions. At meiosis I, the two homologues of each pair separate. At meiosis II, the two sister chromatids of each chromosome separate. Nondisjunction is a failure of chromosomes to part when a cell divides. Where it happens changes the result.

scenes.tts: Follow chromosome twenty-one in one human spermatocyte, and call the father's homologues twenty-one A and twenty-one B. Suppose they fail to separate at meiosis one, so both go to the same cell. Meiosis two runs normally. That cell gives two sperm that are disomic, meaning each has two copies. The other cell has none, so its two sperm are nullisomic.
scenes.caption: Follow chromosome 21 in one human spermatocyte, and call the father's homologues 21A and 21B. Suppose they fail to separate at meiosis I, so both go to the same cell. Meiosis II runs normally. That cell gives two sperm that are disomic, meaning each has two copies. The other cell has none, so its two sperm are nullisomic.
scenes.visual: Both homologues travel to the same cell at meiosis I; meiosis II then gives two sperm holding blue plus yellow, and two empty sperm.
scenes.narration: Follow chromosome 21 in one human spermatocyte, and call the father's homologues 21A and 21B. Suppose they fail to separate at meiosis I, so both go to the same cell. Meiosis II runs normally. That cell gives two sperm that are disomic, meaning each has two copies. The other cell has none, so its two sperm are nullisomic.

scenes.tts: Now fail at meiosis two instead, with meiosis one normal. In one cell the sisters of twenty-one A fail to part, giving one disomic sperm and one with none. The other cell divides normally and gives two normal sperm. So a meiosis one error gives two disomic sperm, and a meiosis two error gives one. Joined to a normal egg, a disomic sperm gives a zygote with three copies.
scenes.caption: Now fail at meiosis II instead, with meiosis I normal. In one cell the sisters of 21A fail to part, giving one disomic sperm and one with none. The other cell divides normally and gives two normal sperm. So a meiosis I error gives two disomic sperm, and a meiosis II error gives one. Joined to a normal egg, a disomic sperm gives a zygote with three copies.
scenes.visual: Homologues separate normally; the two sisters of the blue chromosome stay together, giving one disomic and one empty sperm beside two normal ones; a tally compares 2 and 1; a disomic sperm meets an egg to make three copies.
scenes.narration: Now fail at meiosis II instead, with meiosis I normal. In one cell the sisters of 21A fail to part, giving one disomic sperm and one with none. The other cell divides normally and gives two normal sperm. So a meiosis I error gives two disomic sperm, and a meiosis II error gives one. Joined to a normal egg, a disomic sperm gives a zygote with three copies.

scenes.tts: The two errors leave different fingerprints near the centromere, because at an informative marker the homologues differ there and sisters usually do not. Take a DNA marker tightly linked to the centromere of chromosome twenty-one. The father carries alleles one and two, and the mother carries three and four. Child A types one, three, four: one paternal allele, but two different maternal alleles. The extra chromosome is maternal and carries both of her homologues, so the error was at maternal meiosis one.
scenes.caption: The two errors leave different fingerprints near the centromere, because at an informative marker the homologues differ there and sisters usually do not. Take a DNA marker tightly linked to the centromere of chromosome 21. The father carries alleles 1 and 2, and the mother carries 3 and 4. Child A types 1, 3, 4: one paternal allele, but two different maternal alleles. The extra chromosome is maternal and carries both of her homologues, so the error was at maternal meiosis I.
scenes.visual: A pair of homologues with different marker alleles beside a pair of sisters with the same one; then father 1,2 and mother 3,4 and Child A with 1,3,4, the two maternal ones circled.
scenes.narration: The two errors leave different fingerprints near the centromere, because at an informative marker the homologues differ there and sisters usually do not. Take a DNA marker tightly linked to the centromere of chromosome 21. The father carries alleles 1 and 2, and the mother carries 3 and 4. Child A types 1, 3, 4: one paternal allele, but two different maternal alleles. The extra chromosome is maternal and carries both of her homologues, so the error was at maternal meiosis I.

scenes.tts: Child B types one, three, three: two copies of one maternal allele. The sisters stayed together, which is consistent with maternal meiosis two. One caveat. A crossover between the marker and the centromere can make sisters differ, so one error can look like the other. Keep the rule: two homologues together point to meiosis one, and two sisters together point to meiosis two.
scenes.caption: Child B types 1, 3, 3: two copies of one maternal allele. The sisters stayed together, which is consistent with maternal meiosis II. One caveat. A crossover between the marker and the centromere can make sisters differ, so one error can look like the other. Keep the rule: two homologues together point to meiosis I, and two sisters together point to meiosis II.
scenes.visual: Child B shows 1,3,3 with the two matching chromosomes bracketed as sisters; a crossover flips one marker; the two fingerprints end side by side as the rule.
scenes.narration: Child B types 1, 3, 3: two copies of one maternal allele. The sisters stayed together, which is consistent with maternal meiosis II. One caveat. A crossover between the marker and the centromere can make sisters differ, so one error can look like the other. Keep the rule: two homologues together point to meiosis I, and two sisters together point to meiosis II.
